newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALPINE SKIING-UNSTOPPABLE SYKORA WINS IN STYLE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-UNSTOPPABLE SYKORA WINS IN STYLE.

text.p: Unstoppable Austrian Thomas Sykora was in a class of his own once again as he cruised to his third successive World Cup slalom win on Sunday.
While his rivals struggled on a piste hardened by cold temperatures, Sykora mastered the conditions to take victory by a massive 1.66 seconds over compatriot Thomas Stangassinger.
"I'm not getting tired of winning," he said. "Every time is different. I've got no explanation for the form I'm in. It's just great."
Almost effortlessly on a sunny day in Chamonix, the tall, stylish Austrian clocked an aggregate winning time of one minute 56.38 seconds to move closer to final victory in the slalom World Cup.

Most of his winning margin came from the first leg which he won by more than a second from Italian Alberto Tomba, who then dropped out with flu to leave Sykora with a lead of 1.17 seconds to take into the second leg.
Sykora, who has won four of the five slaloms held so far this winter while finishing second in the other, dominates the slalom the way the great Tomba once did.
Tomba decided after the first leg that he would be better off spending the rest of the day in bed in an attempt to be fit for his next race, a giant slalom on Tuesday in Adelboden, Switzerland.

Third place went to unheralded Swede Martin Hansson, who earned the first podium place of his career with an aggregate time of 1:58.40, a fast second leg boosting him from his first-leg position of 15th.

The 28-year-old Sykora, who had not won anything until he tamed the famed Kitzbuehel piste in a slalom last year, recorded his sixth World Cup win and has appeared on the podium in each of his last nine races.
Olympic champion Stangassinger said he had no other option than taking risks in the second leg after finishing a modest seventh in the first.

"I'm very pleased with my second leg," he said. "If I manage to race in both legs like I did in the second, maybe I can win a race. But the way Thomas is skiing at the moment, he's almost unbeatable."
Sykora, who holds a comfortable lead of 200 points on second-placed Stangassinger in the slalom World Cup standings with four races remaining, said he was not taking anything for granted.

"Thomas (Stangassinger) is dangerous because he's very consistent," he said. "It might look like nothing can happen to me but it will not last for ever. You never know, in the next race, I might straddle a gate."
Giant slalom specialist Michael von Gruenigen of Switzerland came fourth to take first place in the overall World Cup standings from Austrian Hans Knauss, who skied out in the second leg.

"I'm delighted because one of my goals this season was to do well in slaloms," he said. "I'm not bothered about the World Cup as I can't possibly win it because I only enter two events (the giant slalom and the slalom). I don't want to think about it. What I'm looking forward to is the race in Adelboden. To win there before my fans would be fantastic."

Knauss, who does not usually race slaloms, took part because he hoped to score points in the weekend's first combined event of the season, based on Sunday's race and Saturday's downhill in this ski village under the Mont Blanc mountain.
Austrian Guenther Mader won the combined event ahead of Norway's Kjetil-Andre Aamodt and Swiss Bruno Kernen.

"I'm delighted because my preparation to the season was hampered by injury," said Mader, one of the few true all-rounders left in the sport. "This win will give me greater confidence for the upcoming races."
